reason: Perianth bristle (sedges) is smooth or barbed. The one example naming the part is correct. The bare 'smooth' examples are assigned by context.
The number of microsporangia (4-7) is a count. This is an ordinary 'amount' pattern.
The coma (hair tuft on a seed) is persistent or falls off. The examples are correct.
The apex of a flower bud can be blunt. But 'with clavate, blunt tip' and 'rather blunt' may describe another organ. A rule would need the bearer to be explicit ('bud apex blunt').
Involucres (Asteraceae, Euphorbiaceae) are often viscid or sticky. The examples are correct.
The bearer is the gland ('glands subcircular'), mapped to secretory tissue. Shape is meaningful for glands.
Stipules can be lanate, meaning woolly with soft, matted hairs. The examples are correct.
A cupulate (cup-shaped) involucre is a standard description, for example in Asteraceae.
Achenes can be pitted (foveate), as the examples show. One French example, 'une fossette sur chaque face', describes a single pit, which is close enough.
Spathes (pairs or sets) can be equal or unequal in size. This is a size comparison among organs.
A tree can have a columnar habit. The 'crown columnar' example is a slight shift of bearer, but the habit reading is acceptable.

Underleaves are a special ventral leaf type in liverworts, and non-vascular leaf is broader than that. Presence or absence of a leaf type is better handled by a presence/absence rule, or by an underleaf class, than by this pair.
A staminal tube or column can be straight or curved. The examples are correct. 'With a straight margin' is a different bearer, but it is a minority.
A leaf apex can be reflexed. The examples are correct.
PATO_0000001 'quality' is the root class and says nothing. The examples are unrelated (striate, erect, curved, teeth spreading). Each needs its own specific quality.
Wrong reading: 'single' here means one (a count, as in 'cilia single'), not PATO 'simple' (unbranched or unlobed).
An ovary apex or sides can be concave. But 'concave nectaries' describes a different organ. A rule would need the bearer of 'concave' to be the ovary itself and not a part or neighbour.
A corolla lip can be streaked, spotted or striped. These are colour patterns. The examples are correct.
Pedicels and peduncles can be arched, as in 'pendulous on arching pedicels'.
A velvety (velutinous) surface texture of the adaxial leaf surface is meaningful. A few examples describe the hairs, not the surface, but the result is similar.
Wrong reading: 'appressed' describes how the hairs lie on the mericarp. It does not describe the position of the mericarp. The bearer should be the hair or trichome.
Cortex tissue can be mucilaginous, which is the same as mucoid. The negation 'not mucilaginous' is handled by the negation rule.
Pith can be mucilaginous. Same sentence as the cortex pair, and meaningful.
Corona lobes (Asclepiadoideae, Passiflora) can be erect. The examples are correct.
PATO_0000001 'quality' is the root class and carries no information. The examples (superior, wavy hairs, ridged) each need a specific quality.
Offsets and tillers (basal axillary shoots) can be present or absent. This is a meaningful presence/absence statement.
Wrong part: the bowl shape belongs to the cupule or the perianth cup, not to the fruit.
A connective appendage has a length. The examples are correct.
Wrong part: 'areole' here means the cell areolation of a moss or lichen thallus. An areole bud is the cactus meristem, which is unrelated.
Wrong part: a 'girdle' is not part of a seed (it belongs to another structure). The pair rests on a wrong bearer reading.
Staminodes can be divided or dissected into filaments (Passiflora, Parnassia). The examples are correct.
The replum (Brassicaceae) has a shape such as elliptic, obovate or oblong. The examples are correct.
'Enclosed in anther sacs' is a relation between two parts and not a quality of the pollinium alone. A rule would need to say whether such relations are kept, and which part is the bearer.
Peristome teeth can be obtuse at the tip. The examples are correct.
A leaf lamina can be tubular, as in rolled or hollow leaves, or tubular in section.
Perianth or limb lobes can be oblanceolate. The examples are correct.
A flower can be oblique or inclined. Some examples are about the mouth or apex, but those are a minority.
Epicalyx bracts can be hairy (hirsute, stellate). The hair-type examples are correct.
A cupule (Fagaceae) can be saucer-shaped or cup-shaped. The examples are correct.
Filaments can be persistent after the anthers fall. The examples are correct.
Bud scales can be leathery (coriaceous). The examples are correct.
Prickles occur in sparse or dense patterns on stems or internodes. The density belongs to the prickles as a group, which is the usual reading.
A leaf margin can be flat or revolute. The examples are correct.
An involucel has a length. The examples are correct.
Perianth bristles can be persistent. The examples are correct.
Perianth bristles can be straight, curved, contorted or flexuose. 'Retrorsely barbed' is a surface feature, not a shape, but it is a minority.
A nectary or nectar scale has a shape such as reniform or ovate. The examples are correct.
Nectar scales can be oblong. The examples are correct.
A peristome can be long or short. One example ('long transitional zone') is about another part, but most are correct.
The examples describe the keels or margins, not the spathe. The bearer reading is wrong. The statements should go to the margin or keel.
PATO 'optical quality' is a vague parent. The examples are colours of different parts (pale to olive green, blackish). A specific colour and the real bearer are needed, not 'whole plant'.
A corolla lip can be divided or lobed (hypochile and epichile). 'Divided by constrictions' is a loose reading, but it is acceptable.
Tepals can be succulent. The examples are correct.
The examples are about venation, midvein or green zones. The bearer is a part of the bract, not the bract. 'Prominent' belongs to the vein.
Involucral bracts can be spatulate. The examples are correct, including the French ones.
A hilum can be short or long. The examples are correct, including the French ones.
The examples are gametophytes (algae, mosses, ferns). They fit if whole plant covers a gametophyte. A rule would need to say whether gametophyte maps to whole plant or needs its own class.
Stamens can be large. 'Enlarged at base' refers to the filament, but the other examples are on the stamen.
Nodal diaphragms have a thickness in mm. The examples are correct. PATO increased thickness is acceptable, but a plain 'thickness' would be better.
Stem nodes can be banded (red-banded in bamboos or grasses). The examples are correct, including the negated ones.
